tip: Object pronouns go before the verb here: 'te amo', not amo-te. Front placement is the norm in spoken Brazilian.
'De carro' means by car. Portuguese uses 'de' for transport: de onibus, de aviao, but 'a pe' for on foot.
'Gostar' always takes 'de' before what you like: 'gostam de samba'. Dropping the 'de' is wrong.
'Com educacao' literally means with education but here means politely: 'corrigiu com educacao' = corrected politely.
Spoken Brazilian uses the bare verb for commands: 'traz' instead of the textbook 'traga'. Both mean bring.
'Nas' fuses 'em + as' (in/at the): 'nas festas' = at the parties. Portuguese contracts em with articles: em+os=nos, em+a=na.
'Pagar com' means to pay using a method: 'pagar com Pix'. To pay for an item, switch to 'pagar por'.
'Pedir' takes its object directly with no preposition: 'me pediu um favor', unlike English ask for.
'Dever' plus a noun means to owe: 'te devo um favor'. Before a verb, 'dever' means should: devo ir.
'Esperar' means wait for and needs no preposition: 'te espero' = I wait for you. Portuguese omits the for.
'Achar' means to find in the opinion sense: 'te achei engracado' = I found you funny. Use it for impressions.
'Convencer' links to the next verb with 'a': 'convenceu a ir' = convinced to go.
'Duvidar que' expresses doubt and triggers the subjunctive: 'terminem', not terminam.
'Embora' (although) always takes the subjunctive: 'embora tenhamos' = although we have.
'Do' is 'de + o' (of the): 'endereco do restaurante' = the restaurant's address. Portuguese shows possession with 'de', not an apostrophe.
'Dele' means his and follows the noun: 'o carro dele' = his car. It is clearer than the ambiguous 'seu'.
'Emprestar' means to lend, not to borrow: 'nos emprestou' = lent us. For borrowing say 'pegar emprestado'.
'Conselho' is countable here: 'um conselho' = one piece of advice. English advice cannot be counted that way.
'A gente' means we but takes a singular verb: 'a gente reuniu', like ele. Very common in everyday speech.
Brazilians often keep the article before a possessive: 'a minha palavra' = my word. Dropping it is also correct.
'Precisar' takes 'de' before a noun: 'precise de mais tempo' = needs more time. Skipping the 'de' sounds off.
'Antes de' plus an infinitive means before doing: 'antes de sair' = before leaving. With a full clause use 'antes que'.
'E preciso que' states a need and triggers the subjunctive: 'faca', not faz.
'Antes que' takes the subjunctive: 'antes que eu me esqueca' = before I forget.
The ending '-inha' is a diminutive, small or affectionate: 'lembrancinha' = a little souvenir, from lembranca.
'O' is him as a direct object and sits before the verb: 'eu o admiro' = I admire him. Casual speech says 'admiro ele'.
'Lembrar de' means to remind of or remember: 'me lembrou do compromisso' = reminded me of the appointment.
'E possivel que' triggers the subjunctive: 'chova', not chove.
'Basta que' (it is enough that) triggers the subjunctive: 'peca', not pede.
'Caso' means if and takes the subjunctive: 'caso precise' = if you need. It is more formal than 'se'.
'Experimentar' means to try or taste something new: 'experimentar a comida' = try the food. Not the same as tentar.
'Convidar' uses 'para' for the event: 'convidou para o churrasco' = invited us to the barbecue.
'Lhes' means to them and marks the indirect object: 'lhes explicou' = explained to them.
With 'vou' plus an infinitive, the pronoun sits between them: 'vou te buscar' = I'll pick you up.
'Conhecer' means to meet for the first time: 'nos conheceu na faculdade' = we met in college. Reencounter is encontrar.
'Cuide' is the polite command, borrowed from the subjunctive: 'cuide bem' = take good care. Casual speech says 'cuida'.
